idiom_name: ArrayBuffer plus typed-array views typed per field (ArrayBufferLike-generic since TS 5.7)
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds types, not semantics: the layout primitives are JavaScript's, so a data-oriented kernel is typed arrays over one ArrayBuffer, with the compiler keeping the views honest. Since TS 5.7 each typed array is generic over ArrayBufferLike (Float64Array<ArrayBuffer>, Float64Array<SharedArrayBuffer>) - 'each TypedArray now contains a type parameter named TArrayBuffer' - which lets a structure-of-arrays layout be typed distinctly from a shared buffer without casts, and --lib es2024 brings the newer ArrayBuffer/SharedArrayBuffer APIs into the type system. Where records stay objects, type them as a closed interface with number fields (one hidden class in V8, monomorphic access sites) and keep per-record types that differ only by shape out of the hot path. The classic structure being replaced is the object graph: the compiler cannot make it contiguous, only the typed arrays can.
pitfalls: Types do not change the runtime element kind: a number[] stays V8-managed and boxed the same way as in JavaScript; only typed arrays give the packed layout.
Buffer vs ArrayBufferLike mismatches (e.g. Node's Buffer vs Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike>, introduced with the TS 5.7 generics) show up as assignability errors that look unrelated to layout.
Structural typing happily accepts a structurally identical class instance where a plain object is expected, mixing hidden classes and deoptimizing access sites.
as any / non-null assertions around typed-array views hide the alignment and bounds rules (byteOffset must be a multiple of the element size, the view must stay in the buffer).
